kp.:knowledge-point/title: Finding the Equation of the Tangent Line to a Curve at a Point

questions.:question/problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=1.$ Given that the point $P(1,2,4)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=\frac{3x+y}{\sqrt{6xy+{y}^{2}}}$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
questions.:question/worked-solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $x=1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(1,2,4)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(1,2)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}$ at $(1,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(1,2) & =\frac{3(1)+(2)}{\sqrt{6(1)(2)+(2)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{5}{\sqrt{16}} \\  & =\frac{5}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(1,2)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(1,2)}(y-2) \\ z-4 & =\frac{5}{4}(y-2) \\ z & =\frac{5}{4}y+\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,2,4)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=1 \\ z &=\frac{5}{4}y+\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

questions.:question/problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=1.$ Given that the point $P(1,1,0)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=3x+6x\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
questions.:question/worked-solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $y=1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(1,1,0)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1,1)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}$ at $(1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1,1)} & =3(1)+6(1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(1\cdot 1) \\  & =3+6\operatorname{ln}⁡1 \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(1,1)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1,1)}(x-1) \\ z-0 & =3(x-1) \\ z & =3x-3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,1,0)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}y &=1 \\ z &=3x-3\end{aligned}\right.
$$

questions.:question/problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=-2.$ Given that the point $P(4,-2,5)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=y\sqrt{x}$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(4,-2)} & =(-2)\sqrt{4} \\  & =-2(2) \\  & =-4\end{aligned}

$$

questions.:question/problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=2.$ Given that the point $P(-\frac{\pi }{2},2,2\pi )$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\frac{xy}{\pi }$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
questions.:question/worked-solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $y=2.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(-\frac{\pi }{2},2,2\pi )$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(-\pi /2,2)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}$ at $(-\frac{\pi }{2},2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(-\pi /2,2)} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(-\frac{\pi }{2}\right)+\frac{\left(-\frac{\pi }{2}\right)(2)}{\pi } \\  & =-1-1 \\  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(-\pi /2,2)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(-\pi /2,2)}(x-\left(-\frac{\pi }{2}\right)) \\ z-2\pi  & =-2(x+\frac{\pi }{2}) \\ z & =-2x+\pi \end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(-\frac{\pi }{2},2,2\pi )$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}y &=2 \\ z &=-2x+\pi\end{aligned}\right.
$$

questions.:question/problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=2.$ Given that the point $P(2,\frac{\pi }{4},0)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=4\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
questions.:question/worked-solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $x=2.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(2,\frac{\pi }{4},0)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(2,\pi /4)}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(2,\frac{\pi }{4}) & =4\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right) \\  & =4\cdot 1 \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(2,\pi /4)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(2,\pi /4)}(y-\frac{\pi }{4}) \\ z-0 & =4(y-\frac{\pi }{4}) \\ z & =4y-\pi \end{aligned}

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(2,\frac{\pi }{4},0)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=2 \\ z &=4y-\pi\end{aligned}\right.

questions.:question/problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=\sqrt{2}.$ Given that the point $P(\sqrt{2},2,\frac{1}{2})$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=-\frac{2{x}^{2}+y}{{y}^{3}}$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
questions.:question/worked-solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $x=\sqrt{2}.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(\sqrt{2},2,\frac{1}{2})$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(\sqrt{2},2)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}$ at $(\sqrt{2},2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(\sqrt{2},2) & =-\frac{2(\sqrt{2})^{2}+2}{{2}^{3}} \\  & =-\frac{4+2}{8} \\  & =-\frac{3}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(\sqrt{2},2)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(\sqrt{2},2)}(y-2) \\ z-\frac{1}{2} & =-\frac{3}{4}(y-2) \\ z & =-\frac{3}{4}y+2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(\sqrt{2},2,\frac{1}{2})$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=\sqrt{2} \\ z &=-\frac{3}{4}y+2\end{aligned}\right.
$$

questions.:question/problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=-2.$ Given that the point $P(-2,0,8)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+4y+x$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(-2,0)} & =(-2)\operatorname{cos}⁡0+4(0)+(-2) \\  & =-2-2 \\  & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(-2,0)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(-2,0)}(y-0) \\ z-8 & =-4(y-0) \\ z & =-4y+8\end{aligned}

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}$ at $(0.5,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(0.5,2)} & =2+2(2)\operatorname{ln}⁡((0.5)(2))+\frac{1}{0.5} \\  & =2+4\operatorname{ln}⁡1+2 \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line: 

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(0.5,2)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(0.5,2)}(y-2) \\ z-4 & =4(y-2) \\ z & =4y-4\end{aligned}

questions.:question/problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=1.$ Given that the point $P(0,1,2)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
questions.:question/worked-solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $y=1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(0,1,2)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(0,1)}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(0,1)} & =(0)^{2}+(1)^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡(0+1) \\  & =1-\operatorname{ln}⁡1 \\  & =1-0 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(0,1)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(0,1)}(x-0) \\ z-2 & =1(x) \\ z & =x+2\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}y &=1 \\ z &=x+2\end{aligned}\right.
$$

questions.:question/problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=0.$ Given that the point $P(\frac{1}{2},0,1)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=(y+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)+2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
questions.:question/worked-solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $y=0.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(\frac{1}{2},0,1)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(\frac{1}{2},0)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}$ at $(\frac{1}{2},0)\,:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(\frac{1}{2},0)} & =(0+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi \cdot \frac{1}{2})+2\cdot \frac{1}{2}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi \cdot 0)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi \cdot \frac{1}{2}) \\  & =1\cdot 0+2\cdot \frac{1}{2}\cdot 1\cdot 1 \\  & =0+1 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(\frac{1}{2},0)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(\frac{1}{2},0)}(x-\frac{1}{2}) \\ z-1 & =1(x-\frac{1}{2}) \\ z-1 & =x-\frac{1}{2} \\ z & =x+\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(\frac{1}{2},0,1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}y &=0 \\ z &=x+\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

canonical.:question/problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=\pi.$ Given that the point $P(1,\pi,-1)$ lies on $C,$ and that $f_x = y\cos(xy) + \cos y,$ find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
canonical.:question/worked-solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z = f(x,y)$ with the plane $y=\pi.$ So, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(1,\pi,-1)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\dfrac {\partial z} {\partial x} \Bigg|_{(1,\pi)}.$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\dfrac {\partial z} {\partial x}$ at $(1,\pi)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1,\pi )} & =\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(1\cdot \pi )+\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi  \\  & =\pi (-1)+(-1) \\  & =-\pi -1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(1,\pi )} & =\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1,\pi )}(x-1) \\ z-(-1) & =(-\pi -1)(x-1) \\ z+1 & =(-\pi -1)x+\pi +1 \\ z & =-(\pi +1)x+\pi \end{aligned}
$$

The equation above represents a line in the $xz$-plane. The $xz$-plane through the point $P(1,\pi,-1)$ has the equation $y=\pi.$

So, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,\pi,-1)$ is given by the intersection of the following planes:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}y &=\pi \\ z &=-(\pi +1)x+\pi\end{aligned}\right.
$$
